basics.title: The Four Tones
basics.subtitle: 第一课 · 四声
basics.explanation: Mandarin is a tonal language — the same syllable said with a different pitch pattern is a completely different word. Get comfortable with tones early, since every word in this app (and in Chinese) depends on them.

points.label: 1st tone — high and flat
points.detail: Your pitch stays level and high the whole time, like holding a note while singing.

points.label: 2nd tone — rising
points.detail: Your pitch rises, like asking "what?" in English.

points.label: 3rd tone — dips then rises
points.detail: Your pitch dips low, then comes back up — like a skeptical "hm?"

points.label: 4th tone — sharp and falling
points.detail: Your pitch drops fast, like giving a firm command: "No!"

points.label: Neutral tone — light and short
points.detail: No strong pitch at all — quick and unstressed, often on a second syllable.

practice.question: Which tone stays high and flat the whole time?
Which tone dips down, then rises back up?
Which tone drops sharply, like a firm "No!"?

basics.title: Reading Pinyin
basics.subtitle: 第二课 · 拼音
basics.explanation: Pinyin uses the English alphabet, but the letters don't always sound like they do in English. A few sounds trip up almost every beginner — here are the ones worth learning early.

points.label: q sounds like "ch"
points.detail: 请 (qǐng) sounds close to "ching," not like an English "q."

points.label: x sounds like a soft "sh"
points.detail: 谢谢 (xièxie) — softer and further forward in the mouth than English "sh."

points.label: zh / ch / sh are retroflex
points.detail: Curl your tongue tip back slightly — 中 (zhōng), 吃 (chī), 是 (shì).

points.label: z / c / s are flat-tongued
points.detail: No curling — 在 (zài), 才 (cái), 三 (sān). Easy to confuse with zh/ch/sh.

points.label: ü is not the same as u
points.detail: Say "ee" with rounded lips — 女 (nǚ). Written as ü, or sometimes just u after j/q/x/y.

practice.question: The pinyin "q" sounds closest to which English sound?
For zh/ch/sh, what do you do with your tongue?
Which pair is easy to confuse with zh/ch/sh?

basics.title: Pronouns & 是 Sentences
basics.subtitle: 第三课 · 代词与「是」
basics.explanation: The most basic sentence pattern in Chinese: [Subject] 是 [Noun] — "X is Y." Once you have pronouns and 是, you can make a huge number of simple sentences.

points.label: 我 / 你 / 他 / 她
points.detail: I, you, he, she — the core singular pronouns.

points.label: Add 们 for plural
points.detail: 我们 (we), 你们 (you all), 他们 (they) — 们 turns a pronoun plural.

points.label: 是 = to be
points.detail: [A] 是 [B] simply means "A is B" — no extra words needed.

points.label: 不是 = to not be
points.detail: Just add 不 before 是 to negate it — 不是 = "is not."

examples.pinyin: wǒ men shì dì xiōng zǐ mèi。
examples.english: We are brothers and sisters (in Christ).

examples.pinyin: tā shì wǒ de péng yǒu。

basics.title: Yes/No Questions & Question Words
basics.subtitle: 第四课 · 疑问句
basics.explanation: Turning a statement into a question in Chinese is simple — no word order changes needed, unlike English.

points.label: Add 吗 for yes/no questions
points.detail: 你是学生。 → 你是学生吗？ Just add 吗 to the end — nothing else changes.

points.label: Question words replace the answer
points.detail: Unlike English, the question word sits exactly where the answer would go: 你是谁？ (literally "you are who?")

points.label: 谁 / 什么 / 哪里
points.detail: who / what / where

points.label: 什么时候 / 为什么 / 怎么
points.detail: when / why / how

examples.pinyin: nǐ jiào shén me míng zì？
xǐ shǒu jiān zài nǎ lǐ？
nǐ wèi shén me chí dào？

practice.question: What word turns a statement into a yes/no question?
In "你是谁？" (you are who?), where does the question word go?
options: Exactly where the answer would go
practice.answer: Exactly where the answer would go

basics.title: Numbers 0–100
basics.subtitle: 第五课 · 数字
basics.explanation: Chinese numbers follow a simple, logical pattern once you know 0–10 — much more regular than English.

points.detail: 零 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九 十

points.label: 11–19: 十 + digit
points.detail: 十一 (11) = ten-one, 十五 (15) = ten-five.

points.label: 20, 30...: digit + 十
points.detail: 二十 (20) = two-ten, 三十 (30) = three-ten.

points.label: 21, 35...: digit + 十 + digit
points.detail: 二十一 (21) = two-ten-one, 三十五 (35) = three-ten-five.

points.label: 100: 一百
points.detail: 一百 = one hundred. The same building-block pattern continues from there.

basics.title: Measure Words
basics.subtitle: 第六课 · 量词
basics.explanation: In English, some nouns need a "counting word" — "a PIECE of paper," "a CUP of tea." In Chinese, almost every noun needs one. This is one of the biggest adjustments for English speakers.

points.label: Pattern: number + measure word + noun
points.detail: You can't just say "number + noun" like in English — a measure word always goes between them.

points.label: 个 — the all-purpose one
points.detail: Used for people and many generic objects when you're not sure which measure word fits.

points.label: 位 — polite, for people
points.detail: 一位牧师 (one pastor) — more respectful than 个 when referring to people.

points.label: 本 — for bound things
points.detail: 一本圣经 (one Bible), 一本书 (one book).

points.label: 杯 — for cups of liquid
points.detail: 一杯茶 (one cup of tea).

practice.question: What goes between a number and a noun in Chinese?
Which measure word is used for a Bible or book?
Which measure word is more polite, for people?
Which measure word works as a general, all-purpose choice?

basics.title: 的 (Possession) & Negation
basics.subtitle: 第七课 · 「的」与否定
basics.explanation: 的 marks possession — like English's "'s." And Chinese has two different negation words that beginners often mix up: 不 and 没(有).

points.label: 的 = possessive marker
points.detail: 我的 (my/mine), 你的 (your/yours), 老师的书 (the teacher's book).

points.label: 不 negates most verbs and adjectives
points.detail: 不是 (is not), 不好 (not good), 不去 (not going).

points.label: 没(有) negates possession and past actions
points.detail: 没有钱 (don't have money), 没吃饭 (haven't eaten) — 没 pairs with 有 or completed actions, not with 是.

points.label: The key distinction
points.detail: 不是 = "is not" ✓ — but 没是 is wrong. 没有 = "don't have" ✓ — but 不有 is wrong.

practice.question: Which negation word pairs with 是?
How do you say "I don't have time"?

basics.title: 了 / 在 / 过 — Talking About Time
basics.subtitle: 第八课 · 时态标记
basics.explanation: Chinese doesn't change verb endings the way English does ("eat" → "ate"). Instead, small marker words show when something happens. These three trip up almost every beginner.

points.label: 了 — completed action
points.detail: 我吃了 (I ate / I have eaten) — marks that the action is done.

points.label: 在 — ongoing action (or location)
points.detail: 我在吃 (I am eating, right now) — or 我在家 (I am at home).

points.label: 过 — past experience
points.detail: 我去过中国 (I have been to China before) — marks "have done this at some point," not necessarily recently.

points.label: Side by side
points.detail: 我吃了 = I ate (done). 我在吃 = I'm eating (now). 我吃过 = I've eaten (that dish) before (experience).

examples.english: I am reading the Bible (right now).
I have read the Bible before (at some point).

practice.question: Which marker shows an action is completed?
Which marker shows an action is happening right now?
Which marker means "have done this before, at some point"?
你受洗了吗？ is asking about...
